sections.heading: 1. 3rd-Declension Nouns — Introduction
sections.content: The 3rd declension is the largest and most varied declension in Greek. Unlike the 1st and 2nd declensions, 3rd-declension nouns have stems that end in consonants or in certain vowels. The nominative singular must be memorized; the other forms are built from the genitive stem.

examples.note: he guards him through the night (genitive of time)

sections.heading: 2. Neuter 3rd-Declension Nouns — σῶμα, πῦρ, ὕδωρ
sections.content: Several important neuter nouns belong to the 3rd declension. Like all neuters, their nominative and accusative are identical. The stem is found by removing -ος from the genitive.

sections.heading: 3. Present Active Indicative — Full Paradigm
sections.content: Now that we have seen 1st and 3rd person singular and 3rd person plural, here is the complete present active indicative for a regular -ω verb.

sections.heading: 4. The Verb εἰμί — Full Present Paradigm
sections.content: The verb εἰμί ("to be") is highly irregular. Its forms must be memorized. Note that most forms are enclitic (they lean on the preceding word for accent) except εἶ (2nd singular) and εἰσί (3rd plural).

sections.heading: 5. New Prepositions: πρός, μετά, περί, κατά
sections.content: This chapter introduces four more prepositions. Like all Greek prepositions, they govern specific cases which determine their meaning.

table.caption: New Prepositions
rows: ἔρχεται πρὸς αὐτόν — he comes to him
μένει μετὰ τῶν τέκνων — he remains with the children
λέγει περὶ τοῦ θεοῦ — he speaks about God
κατὰ τὸν νόμον — according to the law

sections.heading: 6. Negation — οὐ and μή
sections.content: Greek has two negative particles. οὐ (οὐκ before vowels, οὐχ before rough breathing) is used with the indicative mood. μή is used with all other moods (infinitive, imperative, subjunctive, etc.).

examples.note: he does not have peace (negating indicative)
he does not want to flee (negating infinitive)

sections.heading: 7. Dative of Manner
sections.content: The dative case can express the manner in which an action is done, without a preposition. This is common with abstract nouns.

examples.note: he is full of/with joy (dative of manner)

sections.heading: 8. The Conjunction ὅτε ("when") and Temporal Clauses
sections.content: ὅτε introduces a temporal clause ("when…"). The verb in the ὅτε clause takes the indicative mood when referring to a definite past or present time.

examples.greek: ὅτε τελεῖ τὸ δεῖπνον, ἅπτει τὸν λύχνον
examples.note: when he finishes the meal, he lights the lamp

examples.greek: ὅτε ἔρχεται ὁ λύκος, φεύγει τὰ πρόβατα
examples.note: when the wolf comes, the sheep flee
